routes.description: Establish that the universe, life, rationality, morality, and human experience are jointly more intelligible as products of a personal creator than of unguided natural processes alone.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its positive indicators support creative intelligence, naturalistic alternatives do not exhaust their explanatory force, and further evidence connects that intelligence to Christian theism.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative evidence points beyond atheistic naturalism toward a personal creator and, with additional evidence, toward Christian theism.

centralBridges.description: Explain why rational and mathematical intelligibility is expected if a rational mind grounds the universe.
Show why the origin and semiotic character of biological information require explanation beyond evolutionary transmission and selection.
Ground objective moral significance and personal accountability in a reality deeper than unguided physical processes.
Connect general creator evidence to specifically Christian claims through historical, biblical, experiential, and personal evidence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish explanations by natural mechanism from explanations by personal agency so that the two are not treated as mutually exclusive.
Account for life-permitting cosmic conditions as evidence relevant to whether the universe has an intelligent source.

routes.description: Establish that scientific mechanisms, emergent order, evolved capacities, and evidence-based inquiry can account for the disputed phenomena without adding a supernatural designer or religious authority.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if natural processes provide sufficient explanatory paths, present scientific unknowns do not license supernatural conclusions, and specifically Christian claims lack necessary evidential support.

motionBridge.description: Show that the phenomena named in the motion can be approached through naturalistic explanation without requiring Christian theism.

centralBridges.description: Explain how apparent design, biological complexity, information, and regularities can arise or persist through unguided natural processes.
Justify withholding supernatural conclusions while testable scientific explanations remain open or under development.
Provide an account of moral conduct and reflection based on evolved social dispositions and consideration of consequences.
Require objective support for religious claims beyond their historical influence, psychological comfort, or inherited authority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Apply methodological economy by adding a divine cause only if natural explanation proves insufficient in principle.
Treat natural laws as human descriptions of observed regularities rather than commands that necessarily imply a lawgiver.

sections.title: Design, mechanism, and explanatory method
sections.rationale: This issue establishes whether scientific mechanisms displace a designer, remain compatible with divine agency, or should be pursued without adding a supernatural explanation.

sections.title: Life's origin, evolution, and biological information
sections.rationale: The origin of replication and the status of DNA information determine whether evolutionary and chemical processes suffice or whether biological organization points to intelligence.

sections.title: Cosmic origin, laws, and life-permitting conditions
sections.rationale: This issue bears on whether mathematical structure, existence, natural regularities, and life-permitting conditions require creative intelligence or admit a naturalistic ultimate account.

sections.title: Morality, responsibility, and ultimate hope
sections.rationale: The competing accounts must explain moral judgment and responsibility, while claims about death and ultimate justice test what each worldview permits beyond present biological life.

sections.title: Historical and experiential grounds for Christian belief
sections.rationale: General arguments for intelligence do not alone establish Christianity, so the route requires assessment of historical and experiential evidence against naturalistic objections to religious authority and conditioning.

routes.description: Infer a supernatural, intelligent, and moral creator from features of reality, then connect that creator specifically to the biblical God through Jesus.

motionBridge.description: The inferred creator must be identified with the God of the Bible rather than only an unspecified supernatural cause.

centralBridges.description: The universe's existence and beginning must require a cause beyond physical matter.

Objective moral obligations must require a personal moral source beyond naturalistic preference.
The historical case concerning Jesus must support resurrection and divine identity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Human fallibility must remain compatible with knowledge of burden-relevant foundational truths.
Suffering must be compatible with divine goodness through a coherent redemptive or ultimate account.

Biblical revelation and resurrection claims must withstand comparison with informed disagreement and rival traditions.
Apparently gratuitous innocent suffering must be reconciled with the claimed omnipotent and benevolent God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Finite human access to objective truth must warrant intellectual humility and revisability.
Methodological naturalism must provide a workable standard for detecting causal interaction and comparing explanations.

routes.description: Establish historical reliability through a cumulative standard that permits ordinary reporting variation while requiring substantial accuracy across the Gospels' claims.
routes.successCriteria: Show that verified or conceded claims at several levels outweigh alleged errors and that prominent discrepancies can arise from historically permissible conventions or reconcilable sequences.

motionBridge.description: The Gospels remain historically reliable if their supported historical content is not counterbalanced by established errors.

centralBridges.description: Identify substantial accurate content among major, intermediate, and lesser Gospel claims.
Show that the principal birth and resurrection differences do not negate the shared central claims or require incompatible histories.
Establish a historically supportable continuity between Synoptic material and claims about Jesus' elevated or divine identity.
Provide a plausible account of how traditions and sources preserved the essential events and teachings reported by the evangelists.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish selection, paraphrase, topical ordering, and approximation from factual contradiction.
Connect disputed material to eyewitnesses, remembered traditions, or sources close to eyewitness testimony.

routes.description: Establish historical unreliability in important respects by locating conflicts or inventions in major narratives and sayings rather than merely peripheral details.
routes.successCriteria: Show that major birth, resurrection, and self-presentation material cannot all be historically accurate and that authorial reshaping or unstable transmission explains the divergences.

motionBridge.description: The Gospels are historically unreliable in important respects if major reported events or sayings contain unresolved conflicts or nonhistorical material.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate materially incompatible historical sequences within the canonical birth narratives.
Demonstrate materially incompatible locations, instructions, or actions within the resurrection narratives.
Show that John's divine self-presentation lacks adequate continuity with earlier Synoptic portrayals of Jesus.
Connect Gospel divergences to evangelists altering inherited material for distinct theological messages and audiences.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Assess whether narrow or nonindependent attestation weakens disputed claims.
Account for how decades of oral transmission and later composition could change reported events or sayings.

sections.title: Standard and cumulative case for reliability
sections.rationale: The governing definition of historical reliability determines whether conceded accuracy across much of Jesus' life can be outweighed by conflicts involving several major narratives or sayings.

sections.title: Historical compatibility of the birth narratives
sections.rationale: Matthew and Luke are the canonical sources that narrate Jesus' birth, so the compatibility and provenance of their family movements bear directly on a principal alleged instance of unreliability.

sections.title: Compatibility of the resurrection accounts
sections.rationale: The resurrection is a central Gospel claim, making the chronology and locations of the women's report, appearances, and disciples' movements material to the reliability question.

sections.title: Jesus' self-presentation and divine identity
sections.rationale: Whether John's divine self-identifications preserve Jesus' historical teaching depends partly on whether earlier Synoptic traditions contain comparable claims, directly or indirectly.

sections.title: Ancient composition and transmission
sections.rationale: The reliability inference depends on whether variation reflects permissible ancient reporting and stable preservation or instead historical invention, changing oral tradition, and message-driven alteration.

routes.description: Establish that neither determined nor undetermined action gives agents the ultimate authorship required for philosophical free will.
routes.successCriteria: Show that actions arise from force or unchosen wants whose causal histories never terminate in self-created control, while explaining practical agency without ultimate desert.

motionBridge.description: Connect the absence of control over determining causes and desires to the conclusion that voluntary action lacks ultimate authorship.

centralBridges.description: Establish that determined events inherit prior causes while undetermined events are uncontrolled, leaving neither branch as agent-authored control.
Establish that conduct follows either force or motivating wants and that agents do not independently choose the wants governing action.
Trace character and choice through upbringing, genetics, circumstances, and dispositions without reaching a self-created source.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how deterrence, prevention, rehabilitation, and compassion remain available without attributing ultimate moral desert.
Account for moral motivation and social restraint through causally formed desires rather than an independently chosen will.

routes.description: Establish that determined agents can possess meaningful freedom when conduct belongs to them, is voluntary, and lacks relevant coercive constraints.
routes.successCriteria: Show that freedom need not require ultimate self-creation, that voluntary agency admits context-sensitive degrees, and that causal description does not exhaust personal or ethical meaning.

motionBridge.description: Connect attributable, voluntary, and substantially unconstrained conduct to a defensible form of freedom despite causal determination.

centralBridges.description: Preserve a meaningful distinction between compelled conduct and action attributable to the person as its relevant source.
Explain freedom and its absence through degrees of voluntary control and context-sensitive impediments rather than causation alone.
Establish that interpersonal responsibility and first-person agency contain semantic and ethical dimensions not exhausted by third-person causal description.
Show how action may genuinely belong to a person while also arising through processes that the person did not deliberately manufacture.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the nonreductive account by treating conscious understanding as temporally and socially constituted rather than a static internal object.
Preserve the richer normative meaning of moral intuition against reduction to psychological or evolutionary causation.
